title: The search for an alternative to plastic

paragraphs.text: Plastic is involved in nearly every part of our lives, from our cars down to our toothbrushes. The first man-made plastic was introduced in 1862 and since then chemical improvements have led to an explosion in new forms of plastic. Once regarded as wonder-materials, they are still ubiquitous but find less favour than they used to. This is because of the very stability and persistence that won them plaudits in the first place. Persistence is not a quality to be desired in something that gets thrown away. Therefore, as so much plastic is used in packaging and in articles that are disposable, many people now see conventional petrochemical plastics as a nuisance and a threat.

Faced with landfills full of slowly rotting plastic, scientists are keen to come up with alternatives that might possibly alleviate the devastating impact plastic is having on our environment. One way to counter this problem is to alter the composition of plastic and produce biodegradable alternatives. One possibility has recently been explored by David Schiraldi of Case Western Reserve University, in Ohio, and his colleagues. They propose to reach back into history and revive the use of a raw material that was used to make some of the first plastics invented: milk.

What they actually suggest is using casein, the principal protein found in cow's milk, which is also used in making adhesives and paper coating. In 1889 a French chemist called Jean-Jacques Trillat discovered that if casein is treated with formaldehyde the result is a hard, shiny substance that does well as a substitute for materials like ivory and tortoiseshell. So widespread was the enthusiasm for the new material that a member of the British royal family ordered several pieces of jewellery made from it. However, casein-based plastic of this sort is too brittle for use in the home. It was eventually superseded by the modern, petrochemical variety, and manufacture had stopped altogether by the 1970s.

Despite this, the thought of reviving it has never quite gone away, and these days the fact that it is made mostly of protein, which decomposes easily, is regarded as a virtue. However, the issue of its structural weakness had to be overcome, because casein is not very strong and water can wash it away. Dr Schiraldi's approach does this by using clay as a skeleton that holds the plastic together.

The clay is freeze-dried into a material resembling a sponge. This material is known as an aerogel and although structurally beautiful, aerogels are famously fragile. This is because what makes them so useful in the production of this plastic is that they are mostly empty space. Indeed, they are sometimes nicknamed 'solid smoke'. Surprisingly, this fragility disguises an underlying stiffness. Stuffing the pores in the aerogel with plastic should remove its fragility and, conversely, the network of clay molecules in the aerogel will stop the plastic cracking. So the researchers reckoned that if they mixed casein with the clay and added glyceraldehyde (which substitutes for the poisonous formaldehyde used in the original plastic), they might be able to make something really rather useful.

To test their ideas the team mixed a solution of casein with glyceraldehyde and the clay, and vigorously stirred the result to get rid of the bubbles, before freezing it at 80°C below zero. Once frozen, the material was placed in a dryer that took all the water from it over the course of four days. It was then cured for 24 hours in an oven at 80°C above zero.

The researchers report that their new ultra-light material matches the stiffness, strength and compressibility of polystyrene, a common packaging material that takes a long time to decompose. However, unlike polystyrene, this new material decomposes once it has been dumped. It is this speed of decomposition that makes it such a good alternative to the conventional plastics which clog landfills the world over. An initial experiment suggested that if left at a dump 20% of it vanished within 18 days. Encouraging findings such as these will hopefully inspire other researchers to improve something that is such a vital yet environmentally evil feature of our modern lives.
